comparisons.peer_topic: 2024 Provision for Credit Losses drivers and amount
comparisons.peer_summary: The provision for credit losses increased $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by credit card and small business loan growth, as well as asset quality deterioration in commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Bank of America reported increases in their 2024 provision for credit losses, with credit card portfolios identified as a primary driver for both institutions. Citi stated its provision rose to $10.1 billion, driven by higher net credit losses in Branded Cards and Retail Services in USPB due to vintage maturation and macroeconomic pressures. Similarly, Bank of America reported a $1.4 billion increase to $5.8 billion, primarily driven by credit card and small business loan growth, along with asset quality deterioration in credit card portfolios. Both disclosures highlight the impact of credit card loan growth and vintage/asset quality deterioration on the provision expense.

sentences.text: Citi's total provisions for credit losses and for benefits and claims was $10.1 billion, compared to $9.2 billion in the prior year.
The increase was driven by higher net credit losses in Branded Cards and Retail Services in USPB, reflecting the continued maturation of multiple cards loan vintages originated in recent years.
The provision for credit losses increased $1.4 billion to $5.8 billion for 2024 compared to 2023.

The provision for credit losses for 2024 was primarily driven by credit card as well as small business loan growth, and asset quality deterioration in the commercial real estate office and credit card portfolios.

comparisons.peer_summary: Provision for credit losses rose to $1.35 billion in 2024 from $1.03 billion in 2023, primarily due to net provisions for the credit card portfolio driven by charge-offs, whereas 2023 included wholesale loan impairments and offsets from portfolio sales.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and Goldman Sachs reported an increase in their total provision for credit losses in 2024, with net credit losses in the credit card portfolio being a key driver for both. Citi's provision rose to $10.1 billion, citing higher net credit losses in Branded Cards and Retail Services. Goldman Sachs' provision rose to $1.35 billion, reflecting net provisions related to the credit card portfolio primarily driven by net charge-offs. While the absolute amounts and specific business segments (USPB vs. whole firm/platform) differ, the common theme is the increase in provisions attributable to credit card loan performance and charge-offs.

comparisons.peer_topic: Provision for Credit Losses and Allowance Metrics
comparisons.peer_summary: The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion (up from $9.3 billion prior year), reflecting $8.6 billion in net charge-offs driven by Card Services and a $2.0 billion net addition to the allowance, which totaled $26.9 billion at year-end.
comparisons.comparison: Both Citi and JPMorgan Chase reported significant increases in their provision for credit losses in 2024, with Card Services being a primary driver of the increase in net charge-offs for both. Citi reported a rise to $10.1 billion driven by higher net credit losses in Branded Cards and Retail Services due to vintage maturation. JPMorgan reported a provision of $10.7 billion, reflecting $8.6 billion in net charge-offs driven by Card Services, specifically citing the 'seasoning of vintages originated in recent years' as a key factor, paralleling Citi's explanation of 'maturation of multiple cards loan vintages.'

sentences.text: Citi's total provisions for credit losses and for benefits and claims was $10.1 billion, compared to $9.2 billion in the prior year.
The increase was driven by higher net credit losses in Branded Cards and Retail Services in USPB, reflecting the continued maturation of multiple cards loan vintages originated in recent years.

• The provision for credit losses was $10.7 billion, reflecting $8.6 billion of net charge-offs and a net addition to the allowance for credit losses of $2.0 billion. Net charge-offs increased by $2.4 billion, driven by Card Services, reflecting the seasoning of vintages originated in recent years, credit normalization, and balance growth. The net addition to the allowance for credit losses included a net addition of $2.1 billion in consumer, driven by Card Services, and a net reduction of $19 million in wholesale.
The provision in the prior year was $9.3 billion, reflecting $6.2 billion of net charge-offs and a $3.1 billion net addition to the allowance for credit losses.
